lesson.title: The Body's Own Internal Map of Touch and Pain
lesson.summary: Somatosensation is the collection of body senses, including touch, pressure, temperature, and pain, and it depends on a variety of specialized receptors plus a spinal cord mechanism that helps regulate how much pain reaches conscious awareness.
lesson.body:
Somatosensation refers to the group of senses that provide information about the body itself and its contact with the physical world, most notably touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, and pain. Unlike vision or audition, which rely on a single specialized organ, somatosensation depends on a wide variety of receptors distributed throughout the skin, muscles, joints, and internal organs, each tuned to a different kind of physical stimulation. Some receptors respond primarily to light touch, others to steady pressure, others to stretching or vibration, and still others specifically to changes in temperature, and this variety is what allows the skin to distinguish a light breeze from a firm poke from a slow temperature change, even though all three are technically forms of physical stimulation on the same patch of skin.

Pain deserves special attention within somatosensation because it behaves differently from the body's other senses. Pain receptors, sometimes called nociceptors, respond to stimulation intense enough to signal actual or potential tissue damage, whether from extreme pressure, extreme temperature, or tissue injury and inflammation. Unlike a sense such as vision, where sensitivity is largely about detecting a stimulus that already exists in the world, pain has an unmistakably protective function, motivating the body to withdraw from harm and to rest and protect an injured area during healing.

One influential explanation for how pain signals are regulated on their way to conscious awareness is the gate control theory of pain. According to this idea, the spinal cord contains a kind of neurological gate that can either allow pain signals to pass through to the brain or partially block them, and this gate can be influenced both by other types of incoming sensory signals and by signals coming down from the brain itself. This is part of why rubbing or applying pressure to a freshly stubbed toe genuinely seems to reduce the pain, since the additional touch and pressure signals traveling along faster nerve fibers can partially close the spinal gate against the slower moving pain signals arriving from the same general area. It also helps explain why psychological factors such as distraction, stress, or expectation can measurably change how intensely pain is experienced, since the brain itself can send signals downward that adjust how open or closed that spinal gate remains.

As with every other sense discussed alongside somatosensation, each type of somatosensory receptor has a measurable Absolute Threshold, the minimum level of stimulation, whether a certain light touch, a specific temperature change, or a given amount of pressure, needed for detection. These thresholds vary considerably across different regions of the body, which is why fingertips and lips, densely packed with touch receptors, are far more sensitive to light touch than an area like the middle of the back, a difference reflected directly in how much of the brain's sensory cortex is devoted to processing input from each body region.
